note: The bundle-size budget. scripts/measure-bundle-size.ts reads it, and CI fails when a ceiling is exceeded.
Only gzipCeilingBytes is judged against. recordedGzipBytes is what was actually measured when the
ceiling was set, kept as the evidence for it. When a measurement passes its ceiling, answer WHY it grew
before touching either number — never edit a figure to fit a target.
A ceiling is an inequality, not an equality, so a recorded figure can drift for a long time without
anything failing. It has. Re-record them together with the published figures that quote them.
Lessons worth keeping, as opposed to the history of each change, which is in git:
Measure what you SHIP, not what you test. Writing the same feature with `#` private fields cost 302 B
across every entry, because at the ES2020 target TypeScript lowers `#` to WeakMaps and accessor helpers.
The benchmark transpiles with esbuild, which leaves `#` intact, so the measurement showed no difference
at all. A figure taken on a different artefact than the one distributed does not transfer.
Bytes and speed are separate questions and can move in opposite directions. Delegating the record of
declared calls out of the chain removed an object and an array copy per chain step and still made the
gzipped core 18 B LARGER, while the raw bundle got smaller: the object-literal keys that disappeared
compressed well against the rest of the bundle, and the null checks that replaced them do not.
Decide such a change on its design, and record the measurement either way.
Do not publish a figure that cannot be reproduced. A row measuring "core plus a bundle of 49 plugins"
was dropped because no record of WHICH 49 survived. An unreproducible number is worse than a missing one.
Anything published elsewhere should be read from here rather than copied. Every figure that was written
by hand into the README or the site has, at some point, been wrong.
HOW TO MEASURE A CHANGE TO THE HOT PATH, because getting this wrong cost most of a day.
Interference on a shared machine is ONE-SIDED: it can only make a sample slower. So the fast
tail is signal and the slow tail is noise about the machine, and the estimator is best-of-N
per side, never the range and never the median.
Measured floor: the SAME code, twelve processes, singleField —
The bottom six sit inside 4.2%. The worst is 2.8x the best. Comparing individual rounds, or
quoting a range, makes every change look unresolvable; comparing best-of-8 resolves about 4%.
Alternate the two sides round by round so machine drift straddles both, take best-of-8 each,
and state the percentage. Below ~4% the answer is 'not measurable here', and that is a real
answer — it was the right answer for the create-rule forwarding closure, which measured
114.4 -> 115.7 ns, i.e. nothing, after a profile had shown its frame at 8.7% of self time.
A frame disappearing from a profile is not a speedup; V8 was already inlining it.
And check the deterministic metric as well: heap delta per call, nine windows with the
scavenged ones dropped, reproduces to 0.8%. It is what catches the case where a change that
cannot possibly be slower is 34x worse because the enclosing function stopped being inlined.

method.measuredFrom: The TypeScript sources under src/, not dist/.
whyNotDist: The package ships unbundled ESM, one module per source file, so the tree actually walked and
pruned is the user's bundler's — the same tree esbuild walks here.
method.entryShape: A synthetic module re-exporting only the named symbols, so only code reachable from those names survives.
method.compression: node:zlib gzipSync at the default level
method.sameAsLegacy: The options match the legacy implementation's own comparison build, without which its published claim cannot be compared against.

ceilingRationale: Ceiling = measured + about 8%. One added plugin costs roughly 200-950 B gzipped, so the
headroom is deliberately smaller than that: adding a plugin must never fit inside the budget

why: The JSON Schema converter stopped trusting the VALUES of the keywords it reads. Twelve
keyword values are checked against the Draft-07 meta-schema at the point each is read —
`type`, `pattern`, `required`, `properties`, `additionalProperties`, `patternProperties`,
`propertyNames`, `dependencies`, `items`, `additionalItems`, `contains` and `uniqueItems` —
and a value the meta-schema forbids raises MalformedSchemaError instead of silently expanding
to no rule at all. `minContains` and `maxContains` became named refusals in the same pass.
The weight is the error class, the value renderer that keeps an untrusted document out of the
message, and one written reason per keyword; none of it is reachable from an entry that does
not take a JSON Schema plugin, which is why the other six entries measure to the byte what
they measured before it.
Paid deliberately: the alternative is a validator that answers `valid` for the inputs its own
document meant to refuse, and nothing downstream can detect that.
About 21 B of the full-feature figure is the price of writing the shared map check ONCE:
`properties` and `patternProperties` had byte-identical bodies, and folding them into one
took 124 B off the RAW bundle while adding to the gzipped one, because duplicated text
compresses almost to nothing and the call that replaced it does not. Kept on the design —
the member sentence is now written once and cannot drift between the two keywords.
The growth above is measured against measuredBeforeGzipBytes — the same three entries,
measured on the same machine from the sources this work started from — and not against the
figures previously recorded here, which sat 22 / 17 / 29 B above what they measured. Those six
other entries keep the recorded figures they had: they drift 2-21 B high for reasons older
than this feature, and re-recording them here would make the cost of the feature unreadable.
Headroom per entry is unchanged (135 / 124 / 107 B), so adding a plugin still cannot fit inside
the budget unnoticed.
Three changes, attributed separately by measuring four trees: the branch point, the branch
point plus each change in turn, and the integrated tree.
The dialect guard is the whole of the movement on the three JSON Schema entries: +838 / +808 /
+871 B, and zero on the other six, which cannot reach it. A document that declares a $schema
Luq has no reading for is refused instead of being read as though it were Draft-07. The case
that forces this is silent and cannot be caught by keyword name: from 2019-09 onward $ref is an
ordinary applicator and its siblings apply, so a 2020-12 document's `{"$ref": ..., "minLength":
5}` lost the minLength with no error and no way to notice.
Of that, about 245 B is the table of written reasons — one sentence per dialect saying what it
does differently. Measured by replacing the sentences with bare names and re-running, and kept:
the sentence is what tells a reader holding a 2020-12 document why a constraint they wrote was
disappearing, and the error is the only place they will be looking.
The slot type guard's six literal codes cost +17 to +22 B on every entry, and the presence
tie-break +36 to +52 B. Both are reachable from the core, which is why the six non-JSON-Schema
entries moved at all; each still fits its existing ceiling and none was raised.
Every recorded figure is re-measured here, including the six that needed no ceiling change.
Those six had drifted 2-21 B above what they measured, for reasons older than this work — the
previous re-record deliberately left that drift alone so the cost of THAT feature stayed
readable. Carrying it a second time would make it permanent, so it is cleared now and stated
instead: of the ~60 B each of those entries moved, 2-21 B is the old drift and the remainder is
the two core changes above.
Headroom on the three raised entries is unchanged at 135 / 124 / 107 B, so adding a plugin
(200-950 B) still cannot fit inside the budget unnoticed.
Two changes, attributed separately by measuring each one alone against the branch point.
+33 B is the IssueCode union: 95 code strings generated from the same catalog as
config/issue-code.lock.json, so a caller can check a switch for exhaustiveness and ask
whether a code came from Luq at all. The runtime half is marked pure and builds its Set on
first use, so a consumer who names only the TYPE carries none of it; what remains is the
re-export binding itself.
+77 B is the per-call allocation work, and it is branches rather than data:
resolveAbortPolicy now recognises the call that overrides nothing and hands back one frozen
policy, and IndexStack builds its two arrays on the first push rather than on every
validate(). A validate() of one string field allocated 144.6 bytes and allocates 40.6.
Paid deliberately. Bytes and allocation move in opposite directions here and the trade is
the right way round: the bytes are paid once when the module loads, and the allocation was
paid on every call the application makes.
Wall-clock is NOT the evidence for this and is not quoted as it. An A/B of four rounds each
on the development machine returned 158.7-194.9 ns against 158.2-187.6 ns — entirely
overlapping, with a spread larger than the change. The allocation figure is a heap delta
over nine windows with the scavenged ones dropped, and reproduces to 0.8%.
Headroom per entry is unchanged (71 / 82 / 79 / 98 / 93 / 81 B), so adding a plugin
(200-950 B) still cannot fit inside the budget unnoticed. The three JSON Schema entries did
not move and keep the ceilings they had.
runField takes one of two routes now, chosen by a flag the plan carries, and the second
route is the bytes. A field that declared nothing but presence and checks was reaching them
through five stages that had nothing to do — applyDefault to be told there is no default,
applyNormalize the same, an empty gate loop, a transform stage validate() never runs, and a
recursion stage holding null. compile-field.ts settles all five once and runField picks.
Measured by A/B, four rounds alternating, best of five samples each: 221.0 / 192.3 / 211.2 /
177.6 ns before against 152.5 / 163.0 / 139.0 / 144.4 after. No round overlaps, which is what
makes it a result rather than a reading — an earlier attempt at this file's sibling produced
158.7-194.9 against 158.2-187.6 and was correctly discarded as unresolvable.
Allocation per validate() of one string field went 40.6 -> 8.5 bytes in the same change, from
IssueSink building its buffer on the first issue rather than on every call.
A warning for whoever edits these paths next, because it cost a day to learn: most of the
allocation V8 reports here is already being ELIDED by escape analysis, and escape analysis
follows inlining. Replacing `issues.some(cb)` with a plain for-loop in create-validator.ts —
strictly less work, no allocation of its own — multiplied the per-call allocation by 34,
because the enclosing function stopped being inlined and everything it had been eliding came
back. Keep the hot functions small, and measure every change, including the ones that cannot
possibly be slower.
Headroom per entry is unchanged, so adding a plugin (200-950 B) still cannot fit inside the
budget unnoticed.
The field list is folded into a chain of closures at build() time, and validate() no longer walks
an array of fields. Measured A/B over fourteen processes a side, alternating, best-of per side:
499.0 -> 395.6 ns on a three-field six-rule shape, which is -20.7%, and 26.7 -> 24.4 bytes per
call. The same rig run on two builds of IDENTICAL code reports -0.1%, so the figure is a result
and not the machine.
The cost is 101 B gzip on core-only, 8698 -> 8799, which is +1.16% of the floor. Bytes are paid
once when the module loads and the walk was paid on every call, so the trade is the same one
recorded on 2026-09-13 and it is the right way round. Every entry moved by about the same amount
because the fold is in the core; a plugin's own bytes did not change.
WHY IT IS WORTH WRITING DOWN, beyond the number. A hand-written validator for the same shape,
held to the same judgements on twelve values, runs at 84 ns — about a sixth of what the plan
costs. Almost all of that gap is the walking, not the rules: a form that keeps every rule behind
an opaque function reference and builds a context object per field, and only writes the field
sequence out straight, measured 92 ns, within 9% of full inlining. V8 inlines the rule calls and
cannot inline away the loop. So plugins do not need to emit source for a compiler to be worth
building later, and this fold is the part of that win available without emitting anything.
It stops at 396 rather than 92 because the fold still calls run-field per field, still builds an
IssueSink, an IndexStack and a run context per call, and still walks the CHECK array inside each
field. Those are the next places to look, in that order.
WHAT THE FOLD REFUSES. foldFields returns null unless every field is plain, and run-plan keeps
its loop when it does. A plain field cannot write back, so the subject cannot move underneath the
chain; anything with a default, a normalizer, a gate, a transform or a recursion takes the
general route unchanged. Nothing here generates code — check:no-dynamic-code still reads this
directory and still reports zero.

crossCheckAgainstDist.why: A record of checking that measuring from src is fair, by bundling a real dist under identical options. Not a gate.
finding: core-only came out within 0.1% either way and six-plugin matched exactly, so measuring src is a
sound proxy for what a user's bundler gets out of dist.
Only the all-plugins entry was larger on the dist side, because that entry lists every public
subpath with export * (including a deprecated alias). That is the entry's shape, not the build's.

legacyBaseline.claim: The legacy README advertised 19-23KB gzipped; 17.4KB of that was the core floor, paid before using anything.

budgets.description: Builder alone: the floor paid by someone who uses no plugin at all.
Builder + required: the point that shows what adding one plugin costs.
Builder + required/stringMin/numberMin: the same set the barrel-equivalence check compares.
Builder + the six plugins of the legacy 'simple' comparison: the direct counterpart to its 19-23KB claim.
Builder + the presence preset (required/optional/nullable): the smallest preset.
Builder + the everyday-rules preset: what a preset costs instead of listing use() calls.
Builder + the jsonSchema plugin alone: the price of taking just the chain method.
Builder + jsonSchemaFullFeature: the price of accepting a whole document.
Builder + every plugin in the catalog, JSON Schema extensions included: the everything ceiling.
